source_refs.note: Chapter 3 exercise (PDF 70-73), solved: 14 MCQs keyed from the chapter (no key is printed), 17 short-answer and 5 descriptive questions with model answers; structures described in words. MCQ I, V and Short (c), (f), (q) carry Book corrections.

blocks.text: Q.1 Four choices are given for each question. Select the correct choice.

blocks.prompt: I. Chemical bond formation takes place when

options.text: force of attraction are equal to the force or repulsion
force of repulsion is greater than force of attraction
force of attraction overcomes force of repulsion

blocks.explanation: A bond forms when the attractive forces (nuclei for electrons) overcome the repulsive forces, so the energy falls and the bonded atoms are more stable than the separate atoms.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (a) is printed “force of attraction are equal to the force or repulsion”; it means “force of attraction is equal to the force of repulsion”.

blocks.prompt: II. An ionic compound A⁺B⁻ is most likely to be formed when

options.text: the ionization energy of A is high and electron affinity of B is low.
the ionization energy of A is low and electron affinity of B is high.
both the ionization energy of A and electron affinity of B are high.
both the ionization energy of A and electron affinity of B are low.

blocks.explanation: An ionic bond forms by complete transfer of electrons from an atom with low ionization energy (A gives A⁺ easily) to an atom with high electron affinity (B gives B⁻ easily) (3.1.1).

blocks.prompt: III. Which of the following molecules has zero dipole moment?
blocks.explanation: BF₃ is trigonal planar and symmetrical; its three B–F bond moments cancel, so its dipole moment is zero. NH₃ (pyramidal), CHCl₃ (unsymmetrical) and H₂O (bent) are polar.

blocks.prompt: IV. The numbers of σ and π bonds in the N₂ molecule are:

options.text: one σ and one π bonds
one σ and two π bonds

blocks.explanation: N≡N is a triple bond: one σ (head-on overlap of 2px) and two π bonds (sideways overlap of 2py and 2pz); bond order 3 (3.6.1).

blocks.prompt: V. Which of the following species has unpaired electrons in antibonding molecular orbitals?
blocks.explanation: N₂²⁻ has 16 electrons, like O₂: its last two electrons go singly into π*2py and π*2pz (Hund), so it has two unpaired antibonding electrons. O₂²⁺ (14 electrons, like N₂) has empty π*; F₂ has π* completely filled (paired); B₂ has its unpaired electrons in bonding π orbitals.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (c) is printed “B”, a boron atom; the molecule meant is B₂. Neither has unpaired electrons in antibonding orbitals, so the answer is unchanged.

blocks.prompt: VI. The shape of ICl₃ according to the VSEPR model is:
blocks.explanation: I has 7 valence electrons: 3 bond pairs (I–Cl) and 2 lone pairs, 5 pairs in all (AB₅ type). The electron pair geometry is trigonal bipyramidal; the two lone pairs sit in the triangle, so the atoms form a T-shape (beyond the chapter, which shows the AB₅ types PCl₅ and I₃⁻).

blocks.prompt: VII. Which of the following shows incorrect bond polarity?
blocks.explanation: Br–Br joins two identical atoms with the same electronegativity, so the bond is non-polar and carries no partial charges (3.1.2). In H–F, Cl–O and C–O the more electronegative atom (F 4.0, O 3.5) is correctly δ−.

blocks.prompt: VIII. Which of the following molecules has a dipole moment?
blocks.explanation: SO₂ is bent (one lone pair on S), so its S=O bond moments do not cancel: 1.61 D. CO₂ and CS₂ are linear and CCl₄ is tetrahedral; their bond moments cancel.

blocks.prompt: IX. How many electrons are present in the valence shell of P in PO₄³⁻?
blocks.explanation:
In the Lewis structure P has one P=O double bond and three P–O⁻ single bonds:
electrons = 2 × (double bond electrons) + 3 × (single bond electrons) = 4 + 3(2) = 10
So P has an expanded octet (by 2), as the chapter lists PO₄³⁻ (3.1.4).

blocks.prompt: X. How many extra electrons than a normal octet are there in the valence shell of I in ICl₅?
blocks.explanation:
I uses 5 of its 7 valence electrons in five I–Cl bonds and keeps one lone pair:
electrons around I = 5 × 2 + 2 = 12
12 − 8 = 4 extra electrons.

blocks.prompt: XI. What is the type and shape of [ICl₄]⁻ according to the VSEPR model?
blocks.explanation: I (7 electrons) + 1 for the charge = 8: four bond pairs and two lone pairs, six pairs in all. Like XeF₄ (3.3.2) it is an AB₆ system: octahedral electron pair geometry, lone pairs at 180°, square planar shape with 90° angles.

blocks.prompt: XII. Which type of hybridization of C occurs in CO₂?
blocks.explanation: C forms two σ bonds (one to each O) and two π bonds and has no lone pair; two electron regions give two sp hybrid orbitals at 180°: linear O=C=O.

blocks.prompt: XIII. Which of the following molecules has a central atom with sp3 hybridization and a tetrahedral electron pair geometry?
blocks.explanation: In CCl₄ carbon forms four σ bonds with sp³ hybrid orbitals: tetrahedral, 109.5° (3.3.2, 3.5.1). BF₃ is sp² (trigonal), SO₂ trigonal (angular), PCl₅ trigonal bipyramidal.

blocks.prompt: XIV. Which of the following species contains a dative bond?
blocks.explanation: In NH₄⁺ the N atom of NH₃ donates its lone pair to H⁺ (which has no electrons), forming a coordinate (dative) bond, like H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺ (3.13). CH₄ and O₂ have normal covalent bonds; NaCl is ionic.

blocks.text: Q.2 Attempt the following short-answer questions:

blocks.prompt:
a. Define the following:
(i) Dipole (ii) Bond order (iii) Permanent dipole- permanent dipole force (iv) London dispersion force
blocks.explanation:
(i) Dipole: a molecule with a partial positive charge (δ⁺) on one part and a partial negative charge (δ⁻) on the other, e.g. Hᵟ⁺–Fᵟ⁻.
(ii) Bond order: the number of bonds between two atoms = (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons)/2; e.g. N₂ = 3.
(iii) Permanent dipole-permanent dipole force: attraction between the δ⁺ end of one polar molecule and the δ⁻ end of a neighbouring polar molecule, e.g. HCl; 5-20 kJ mol⁻¹.
(iv) London dispersion force: weak attraction between an instantaneous dipole in one molecule and the dipole it induces in a neighbour; present in all molecules, e.g. Cl₂, noble gases; 1-20 kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.prompt:
b. Draw the Lewis (electron dot) structures for the following species:
(i) HCN (ii) NCl₃ (iii) CO (iv) O₃ (v) NO₂
blocks.explanation:
(i) HCN (10 valence electrons): H–C≡N: ; one pair H–C, three pairs C≡N, one lone pair on N.
(ii) NCl₃ (26): N in the centre with three N–Cl single bonds and one lone pair; each Cl has three lone pairs.
(iii) CO (10): :C≡O: ; three shared pairs (one of them donated by O, a dative bond) and one lone pair on each atom.
(iv) O₃ (18): O=O⁺–O⁻ ; central O has one lone pair, the double-bonded O two lone pairs, the single-bonded O three lone pairs (the O–O bond is the dative bond).
(v) NO₂ (17, odd electron): O=N–O ; N has one unpaired electron, the double-bonded O two lone pairs, the single-bonded O three lone pairs (N has only 7 electrons).

blocks.prompt:
c. Xenon ist a noble gas (group 18); xenon trioxide has the following structure:
(Structure printed: Xe at the top with one lone pair, joined by double bonds to three O atoms below it.)
i. By counting electron pairs around the central atom, explain why xenon trioxide has this shape.
ii Draw a structure of xenon trioxide showing partial charges on the atoms and the direction of the dipole in the molecule.
blocks.explanation:
i. Xe has 8 valence electrons; 6 are used in three Xe=O double bonds and 2 remain as one lone pair. So there are four electron regions (each double bond counts as one): tetrahedral electron pair geometry. Excluding the lone pair, XeO₃ is trigonal pyramidal, with O–Xe–O angles less than 109.5° (lone pair repulsion).
ii. Draw the same pyramid: Xe at the apex marked δ⁺, each O at the base marked δ⁻ (O is more electronegative). The bond moments add up along the axis; the dipole points from the δ⁺ Xe towards the δ⁻ oxygen base (the book draws dipoles from δ⁺ to δ⁻).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints “Xenon ist a noble gas”; it means “Xenon is a noble gas”.

blocks.prompt: d. Explain the difference between the formation of σ and π bonds.
blocks.explanation: A σ bond forms by head-on overlap on the nuclear axis; a π bond by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals (3.4.1).

rows: Linear (head-on) overlap along the nuclear axis
s-s, s-p, p-p or hybrid orbitals can form it
Only unhybridized p orbitals form it
Electron density on the nuclear axis
Electron density above and below the axis; none on it
Stronger; formed first; single bond is σ
Weaker; forms only after a σ bond (double, triple bonds)

blocks.prompt:
e. The structure of propanone (acetone) is:
(Structure printed: a central C double-bonded to O above it and single-bonded to two CH₃ groups, H₃C and CH₃.)
i. Show how the central carbon atom forms σ and π bonds through hybridization.
ii. Can propanone make a hydrogen bond with water when both are intermixed?
blocks.explanation:
i. The central C is sp² hybridized (2s¹ 2px¹ 2py¹ 2pz¹ → three sp² + one 2pz). The three sp² orbitals (trigonal planar, 120°) form three σ bonds: two with the CH₃ carbons and one with O. The unhybridized 2pz of C overlaps sideways with a 2p orbital of O to form the π bond, so C=O is σ + π.
ii. Yes. The O of C=O is δ⁻ and has two lone pairs, so the δ⁺ H of water forms a hydrogen bond with it (O–H···O=C); this is why propanone mixes with water. (Propanone cannot H-bond with itself: it has no H on O.)

blocks.prompt: f. Predict the shapes of sulfate ([SO₄]²⁻, borate ([BH₄]⁻) and tri-iodide ions ([I₃]⁻) according to the VSEPR model.
blocks.explanation:
[SO₄]²⁻: four S–O bonding regions (two S=O, two S–O⁻), no lone pair: tetrahedral, 109.5°.
[BH₄]⁻: B (3 electrons + 1 for the charge) forms four B–H bond pairs, no lone pair: tetrahedral, 109.5°.
[I₃]⁻: central I has 2 bond pairs + 3 lone pairs (AB₅): trigonal bipyramidal electron pair geometry; lone pairs in the triangle, so the shape is linear, 180°.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: [BH₄]⁻ is printed as “borate”; it is the tetrahydroborate (borohydride) ion. Borate is an oxyanion of boron such as BO₃³⁻. The bracket after “sulfate ([SO₄]²⁻” is also not closed.

blocks.prompt: g. Sketch the molecular orbital pictures of π(2p) and π*(2p).
blocks.explanation:
Draw two parallel 2p orbitals (say 2py) on two nuclei, perpendicular to the nuclear axis.
π(2p), bonding: lobes of the same sign overlap sideways, giving one electron cloud above and one below the nuclear axis, with zero density on the axis (nodal plane); lower energy.
π*(2p), antibonding: lobes of opposite sign combine, giving four separate lobes with an extra node between the nuclei; least density between the nuclei; higher energy.

blocks.prompt: h. Sketch the hybrid orbitals and bond formation in PCl₃, SiCl₄, and NH₄⁺.
blocks.explanation:
PCl₃: P (3s² 3p³) is sp³: four sp³ orbitals, three half-filled overlap with 3p of three Cl (σ), the fourth holds a lone pair: pyramidal, angle less than 109.5°.
SiCl₄: Si (3s² 3p² → excited 3s¹ 3p³) is sp³: four half-filled sp³ orbitals overlap with 3p of four Cl: tetrahedral, 109.5°.
NH₄⁺: N (2s² 2p³) is sp³: three half-filled sp³ overlap with 1s of three H; the lone-pair sp³ is donated to H⁺ (dative bond): tetrahedral, 109.5°, all four N–H bonds alike.

blocks.prompt:
i. The structures of PF₃ and SiF₄ are given below. Redraw these with partial charges and state which is polar and which is non-polar.
(Structures printed: PF₃ with P at the top bonded to three F atoms below it; SiF₄ with Si in the centre bonded to four F atoms.)
blocks.explanation:
PF₃: Pᵟ⁺ with three Fᵟ⁻; P has a lone pair, so the molecule is pyramidal and the bond moments do not cancel: polar.
SiF₄: Siᵟ⁺ with four Fᵟ⁻; the molecule is regular tetrahedral and the four equal bond moments cancel: non-polar.

blocks.prompt: j. Draw the orbital structures of the CO₂ molecule in terms of VBT.
blocks.explanation:
C (excited 2s¹ 2px¹ 2py¹ 2pz¹) is sp hybridized: two sp orbitals at 180° plus unhybridized 2py and 2pz.
σ bonds: each sp orbital overlaps head-on with a half-filled 2p orbital of one O (two C–O σ bonds, linear).
π bonds: C 2py overlaps sideways with 2py of one O, and C 2pz with 2pz of the other O; the two π bonds lie in perpendicular planes. So O=C=O, linear, 180°.

blocks.prompt:
k. Draw the Lewis structures and tell whether these ions involve expanded octets?
i) ClO₄⁻ ii) ICl₄⁻ iii) NH₄⁺ iv) I₃⁻
blocks.explanation:
i) ClO₄⁻: Cl with three Cl=O and one Cl–O⁻ (as the book draws SO₄²⁻): 3(4) + 2 = 14 electrons around Cl: expanded.
ii) ICl₄⁻: I with four I–Cl bonds and two lone pairs: 12 electrons: expanded.
iii) NH₄⁺: N with four N–H bonds, no lone pair: 8 electrons: not expanded (N, period 2, has no d orbitals).
iv) I₃⁻: central I with two I–I bonds and three lone pairs: 10 electrons: expanded.

blocks.prompt: l. The bond between K and Cl is ionic but that between Si and Cl is polar covalent. Explain why.
blocks.explanation:
Electronegativity difference decides the bond (3.2):
K–Cl: 3.0 − 0.8 = 2.2 (above 1.8): electron transferred, ionic.
Si–Cl: 3.0 − 1.8 = 1.2 (between 0.4 and 1.8): electrons shared unequally, polar covalent.

blocks.prompt: m. SO₂ is a polar molecule but SO₃ not. Justify.
blocks.explanation:
SO₂: one lone pair on S makes it angular (V-shaped, less than 120°), so the two S=O bond moments do not cancel: dipole moment 1.61 D, polar.
SO₃: three S=O bonds and no lone pair give a symmetrical trigonal planar shape (120°); the three bond moments cancel: zero dipole moment, non-polar.

blocks.prompt: n. Which of O₂²⁺, and O₂²⁻ would be paramagnetic? Give reason in the light of MOT.
blocks.explanation:
Neither. Using the O₂ order σ2s < σ*2s < σ2px < π2py = π2pz < π*2py = π*2pz:
O₂²⁺ (14 electrons): σ2s² σ*2s² σ2px² π2py² π2pz²; π* empty, all paired: diamagnetic, bond order 3.
O₂²⁻ (18 electrons): … π*2py² π*2pz²; π* full, all paired: diamagnetic, bond order 1.
(O₂, O₂⁺ and O₂⁻ have unpaired π* electrons and are paramagnetic.)

blocks.prompt:
o. Which of the following bonds would be most polar?
i) C-Cl ii) Si-F iii) Se-F
blocks.explanation:
Si–F, because it has the largest electronegativity difference:
C–Cl: 3.0 − 2.5 = 0.5
Si–F: 4.0 − 1.8 = 2.2
Se–F: 4.0 − 2.4 = 1.6 (Se 2.4 is beyond the chapter)

blocks.prompt: p. What are necessary conditions for the hydrogen bond to form?
blocks.explanation:
1. H must be covalently bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom (F, O or N), so it carries a large δ⁺ charge.
2. Another small, highly electronegative atom (F, O, N) with a lone pair must be nearby to attract that H, e.g. in H₂O, HF and NH₃ (details in the chapter on states of matter).

blocks.prompt: q. Compare the bond energies of single, double, and triple bonds between the same two atoms (e.g., H-H, O=O, O≡O). Explain the trend in terms of the number of shared electrons.
blocks.explanation:
Between the same two atoms: triple > double > single, e.g. C≡C 839 > C=C 614 > C–C 347 kJ mol⁻¹ (Table 3.2).
A single bond shares 2 electrons, a double bond 4 and a triple bond 6. More shared electrons between the nuclei give stronger attraction, so more energy is needed to break the bond, and the bond is shorter (C–C 154, C=C 133, C≡C 120 pm). The rise is less than double or triple because π bonds are weaker than the σ bond.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The examples are printed “H-H, O=O, O≡O”. These are not bonds between the same two atoms in one series (H–H is a different pair), and O≡O does not exist: oxygen forms O=O (495 kJ mol⁻¹). A correct series between the same two atoms is C–C, C=C, C≡C (347, 614, 839 kJ mol⁻¹) from the chapter's Table 3.2.

blocks.prompt:
Q.3 How the bonding in the following molecules can be explained with respect to valence bond theory?
(i) Cl₂ (ii) O₂ (iii) N₂ (iv) HF (v) H₂S
blocks.explanation:
VBT: a covalent bond forms when half-filled valence orbitals of similar energy on two atoms overlap; greater overlap gives a stronger bond, and bonds are directional.
(i) Cl₂: Cl = [Ne] 3s² 3px² 3py² 3pz¹. The half-filled 3pz orbitals of two Cl atoms overlap head-on along the nuclear axis (p-p overlap): one σ bond, Cl–Cl. Electron density is symmetrical (same electronegativity): non-polar.
(ii) O₂: O = 1s² 2s² 2px¹ 2py¹ 2pz²(pair). The half-filled 2px orbitals overlap end-to-end: σ bond. The half-filled 2py orbitals are parallel and overlap sideways, above and below the axis: π bond. So O=O (one σ + one π).
(iii) N₂: N = 1s² 2s² 2px¹ 2py¹ 2pz¹. 2px–2px head-on overlap: σ bond; 2py–2py and 2pz–2pz sideways overlaps: two π bonds in perpendicular planes. So N≡N (one σ + two π), a very strong bond.
(iv) HF: the half-filled 1s orbital of H overlaps with the half-filled 2p orbital of F (s-p overlap): σ bond. F is more electronegative, so density is greater near F: Hᵟ⁺–Fᵟ⁻, polar.
(v) H₂S: S = [Ne] 3s² 3px² 3py¹ 3pz¹. The two half-filled 3p orbitals (3py, 3pz, at 90°) each overlap with the 1s orbital of one H (s-p overlap): two σ bonds. The molecule is V-shaped with H–S–H angle 92° (close to the 90° between p orbitals).

blocks.prompt:
Q.4 What are the postulates of VSEPR model? Discuss the structures of the following species with reference to this theory.
(i) CH₄ (ii) NH₃ (iii) H₃O⁺ (iv) PCl₅ (v) SO₂ (vi) SF₆
blocks.explanation:
VSEPR (Sidgwick and Powell, 1940): a molecule takes the shape in which repulsions between the valence electron pairs of the central atom are minimum.
Postulates:
1. Both lone pairs and bond pairs decide the geometry.
2. Electron pairs arrange themselves around the central atom as far apart as possible.
3. Lone pairs occupy more space than bond pairs and compress the bond angles.
4. Order of repulsion: lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair.
5. A double or triple bond is treated as a single electron pair (region).
6. Highly electronegative atoms on the central atom reduce bond pair repulsions.
The electron pair geometry comes from the total pairs; the shape comes from the atoms only (lone pairs excluded).
(i) CH₄ (AB₄, 4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs): tetrahedral, H–C–H 109.5°.
(ii) NH₃ (4 pairs: 3 bond, 1 lone): tetrahedral electron pair geometry, trigonal pyramidal shape, 107°.
(iii) H₃O⁺ (H₂O + H⁺; 4 pairs: 3 bond, 1 lone): tetrahedral geometry, trigonal pyramidal shape like NH₃.
(iv) PCl₅ (AB₅, 5 bond pairs, 0 lone): trigonal bipyramidal; 120° in the triangle, 90° between axial and equatorial bonds.
(v) SO₂ (3 regions: two S=O, one lone pair): trigonal electron pair geometry, angular (V-shaped), angle less than 120°; dipole moment 1.61 D.
(vi) SF₆ (AB₆, 6 bond pairs, 0 lone): octahedral, all F–S–F angles 90°.

blocks.prompt: Q.5 Explain the orbital hybridization for CH₄, NH₃, BF₃, and BeCl₂.
blocks.explanation:
Hybridization: mixing of atomic orbitals of slightly different energies and shapes in one atom to form an equal number of equivalent hybrid orbitals of the same energy and shape.
CH₄ (sp³): C 2s² 2px¹ 2py¹ → excited 2s¹ 2px¹ 2py¹ 2pz¹. One 2s and three 2p mix to four sp³ orbitals, each with one electron, pointing to the corners of a regular tetrahedron. Each overlaps with the 1s of an H (sp³-s): four σ bonds; tetrahedral, 109.5°.
NH₃ (sp³): N 2s² 2px¹ 2py¹ 2pz¹ forms four sp³ orbitals; one holds a lone pair and three are half-filled and overlap with three H 1s orbitals. The lone pair repels the bond pairs: pyramidal, 107°.
BF₃ (sp²): B 2s² 2px¹ → excited 2s¹ 2px¹ 2py¹. One 2s and two 2p mix to three sp² orbitals in a plane at 120°; each overlaps with a half-filled 2pz of F (sp²-p): trigonal planar, 120°; one empty 2p remains on B.
BeCl₂ (sp): Be 2s² → excited 2s¹ 2px¹. One 2s and one 2p mix to two sp orbitals at 180°; each overlaps with a half-filled 3p of Cl: linear Cl–Be–Cl, 180°.

blocks.prompt:
Q.6 Draw the molecular orbital diagrams of the following molecules. Calculate their bond orders?
(i) H₂ (ii) He₂ iii) N₂ (iv) O₂
blocks.explanation:
In each diagram draw the atomic orbitals of the two atoms on the left and right, the molecular orbitals in the middle (bonding lower, antibonding higher), an energy arrow upward, and fill electrons from the bottom (Pauli, Hund).
Bond order = (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons)/2
(i) H₂ (2 electrons): σ1s². Bond order = (2 − 0)/2 = 1 (single bond, diamagnetic).
(ii) He₂ (4 electrons): σ1s² σ*1s². Bond order = (2 − 2)/2 = 0, so He₂ does not form.
(iii) N₂ (valence 10 electrons; 1s electrons ignored): σ2s² σ*2s² π2py² π2pz² σ2px² (order σ2s < σ*2s < π2py = π2pz < σ2px < π*2p < σ*2px). Bond order = (8 − 2)/2 = 3: N≡N, one σ + two π; all paired, diamagnetic.
(iv) O₂ (valence 12 electrons): σ2s² σ*2s² σ2px² π2py² π2pz² π*2py¹ π*2pz¹ (order σ2s < σ*2s < σ2px < π2p < π*2p < σ*2px). Bond order = (8 − 4)/2 = 2: O=O. The two unpaired π* electrons make O₂ paramagnetic (liquid O₂ is held between the poles of a magnet).

blocks.prompt: Q.7 Discuss the formation of F₂ molecule in the light of Lewis concept, VBT, and MOT.
blocks.explanation:
F = 1s² 2s² 2px² 2py² 2pz¹ (7 valence electrons).
1. Lewis concept: each F needs one electron to complete its octet. The two atoms share one pair: F–F, a single covalent bond; each F then has three lone pairs and eight valence electrons (neon configuration). The bond is non-polar (same electronegativity).
2. VBT: the half-filled 2pz orbital of one F overlaps head-on with the half-filled 2pz of the other along the nuclear axis (p-p overlap), forming one σ bond, like Cl₂. The filled 2s, 2px and 2py orbitals stay as lone pairs.
3. MOT: the 14 valence electrons fill σ2s² σ*2s² σ2px² π2py² π2pz² π*2py² π*2pz² (σ*2px empty).
Bond order = (bonding − antibonding)/2 = (8 − 6)/2 = 1: a single bond, as in the Lewis and VBT pictures. All electrons are paired, so F₂ is diamagnetic. The many antibonding electrons explain the weak F–F bond (154 kJ mol⁻¹, Table 3.2).
